signpostPins.title: 1. Learning
signpostPins.body: Learning at university is not the same as at school: more of it is in your hands, and the point is to understand and use ideas, not just collect them. The first two lessons look at what that shift asks of you, and at how each module spells out what you are meant to learn.

signpostPins.title: 2. Assessment
signpostPins.body: Assessment is how your learning is tested, through essays, exams, presentations and more. It is not there to catch you out: it shows you, and your tutors, how your learning is going. The third lesson looks at what assessment is really for, and at how to read what a task is asking of you.

signpostPins.title: 3. Feedback
signpostPins.body: Feedback is what you get back on your work, and it is the part students most often waste. Used well, it is your tutors telling you what to do differently next time. The fourth lesson looks at the forms feedback arrives in, and at how to work out the action a comment is really asking for.

practiceConnection.academic: Everything in this course applies to the work you are already doing. Every module you take sets assessments, marks them against criteria, and gives you feedback; the students who understand that cycle, and run it on purpose, are the ones whose work improves from one assignment to the next rather than repeating the same mistakes. Treat what follows as being about your own essays, reports and exams, not about study in the abstract.
practiceConnection.professional: The same brief, standard, feedback and next-task cycle runs in many areas of professional practice. You are given a brief, your work is judged against a standard, you receive feedback, and you carry it into the next task. Learning from that feedback and iterating your practice on the back of it is a habit you keep long after you graduate.

decidedValue.overview:
Three things shape how you get on at university: how you learn, how you are assessed, and the feedback you get along the way. Most students meet these one at a time and treat them as separate hurdles. This course takes a different view. It shows how learning, assessment and feedback work together as one cycle, and why seeing that connection is what lets you study with purpose rather than just keep up.

Over five short lessons you will look at what learning at university actually asks of you, and at how university spells out what you are meant to learn. You will then look at what assessment is really for, at how to make feedback worth having, and finally at how the three connect into a single cycle you can run deliberately. None of it is abstract: it all applies to the work you are already doing, this term, in whatever you are studying. By the end you will have a clearer picture of how your own studies work, and a few practical habits for making each piece of work feed the next.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming:
By the end of this course you will be able to:

  • apply an understanding of how university learning works to your own study;
  • interpret your own assessment tasks and marking criteria;
  • act on feedback to improve your own work;
  • align your own academic practice with the learning, assessment and feedback cycle.

These matter because none of them belongs to a single module: every subject you take will set work, mark it against criteria, and give you feedback. The sooner you understand how that cycle works, the more each piece of work you do can build on the last.

items.stem: A student says: "I just need to memorise everything the lecturer says and repeat it in the exam." Why is this a weak approach to university learning?

options.text: Because university learning is about understanding and using ideas, not just reproducing them; most assessments reward what you can do with the material.
options.feedback: Yes. University rewards what you can do with ideas, not how much you can repeat.

options.text: Because lecturers do not say anything worth memorising.
options.feedback: No. Lectures are worth attending; the point is to understand, not only memorise.

options.text: Because memorising anything is impossible at university.
options.feedback: No. Memory still matters; it just is not the whole of learning here.

options.text: Because exams never draw on what is covered in lectures.
options.feedback: No. Exams often do draw on lectures, but they ask you to use the material, not just recall it.

feedback.correct: That's right. University learning is about understanding and using ideas, which is what most assessment rewards.
feedback.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what university assessment actually asks you to do with what you learn. Try again.

items.stem: You are starting a new module and want to know what you will actually be expected to be able to do by the end. Where should you look first?

options.text: The module's learning outcomes.
options.feedback: Yes. Learning outcomes state what you should be able to do by the end.

options.text: The total length of the reading list.
options.feedback: No. The reading supports the module, but it does not state what you must be able to do.

options.text: The number of lectures each week.
options.feedback: No. The timetable tells you when you meet, not what you must be able to do.

options.text: The name of the lecturer.
options.feedback: No. Who teaches it does not tell you what you are expected to achieve.

feedback.correct: That's right. A module's learning outcomes tell you what you should be able to do by the end.
feedback.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which part of a module states what you must be able to do. Try again.

items.stem: An essay brief says: "Critically evaluate the two main approaches." What is it mainly asking you to do?
